page: Amazon Web Services r5a.24xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine powered by the Nitro hypervisor and dedicated AMD hardware. The server provides 96 virtual CPUs across 48 physical cores utilizing the AMD EPYC 7571 processor clocked at 2.5 GHz on an x86_64 architecture. Equipped with 768.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, it delivers an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio. The configuration does not include local storage or dedicated GPU acceleration, relying entirely on remote storage, while offering a baseline network bandwidth of 20 Gbps.

Benchmark results highlight significant differences between single-threaded and multi-threaded throughput. Single-core compute capabilities are limited, with stress-ng single-core and Geekbench single-core results placing in the bottom 10 percent of recorded systems. In contrast, multi-core throughput aligns with middle 50 percent averages across stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and multi-threaded decompression tests. Hardware-assisted cryptography demonstrates higher relative throughput, achieving top 25 percent results on the PassMark CPU encryption benchmark. Memory bandwidth is average under large uncached operations at 159.52 GB/sec read and 78.43 GB/sec write, but demonstrates high cached read throughput.

The hardware configuration provides high memory density at a lower price band compared to high-frequency compute alternatives. However, users face a tradeoff between vast memory capacity and modest per-core compute speed. Workload fit includes memory-intensive tasks with moderate single-core demands, such as distributed in-memory caching via Redis, large in-memory databases, extract-transform-load (ETL) processing pipelines, and enterprise enterprise resource planning backends.
description: Amazon Web Services r5a.24xlarge is a memory-optimized Nitro-based instance configured with 96 vCPUs and 48 physical cores on an AMD EPYC 7571 processor running at 2.5 GHz. It features 768.0 GB of DDR4 system memory at 3 GHz, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU, alongside 20 Gbps of baseline network bandwidth without local disk storage or discrete GPUs. Empirical testing reveals modest single-threaded efficiency alongside standard multi-core throughput, supported by strong cryptographic instruction performance via hardware acceleration. The large RAM pool makes this instance a practical choice for cost-conscious, memory-heavy workloads requiring horizontal parallelization rather than peak single-thread execution, including in-memory databases, Redis caches, and batch data processing.
